identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Yamunotri, seat of the river-goddess Yamuna, is one of the four shrines of the Chota Char Dham pilgrimage circuit in the Garhwal Himalaya, standing at roughly 3,293 m in Uttarkashi district. Unlike Badrinath and Kedarnath, it has no state-run shrine board: worship and much of the temple's administration rest with the hereditary Uniyal priest family of Kharsali village. The temple, rebuilt in stone in the 19th century after earlier structures were lost to snow and floods, holds a black marble image of the goddess and stands beside the geothermal Surya Kund. It is a seasonal shrine, open only from around Akshaya Tritiya in spring to shortly after Diwali in autumn; through the winter, worship of the goddess's processional idol continues at Kharsali.

governance.establishedEra: 19th century; sources disagree on the builder and exact year — Maharaja Pratap Shah of Tehri Garhwal per Wikipedia's Yamunotri Temple article and government sources, versus Raja Sudarshan Shah in 1839 per Wikipedia's general Yamunotri article and CPREEC (see documented history). The temple has been destroyed and rebuilt at least twice after snow and flood damage.
governance.managingAuthority: Administered day to day as the 'Yamunotri Temple Committee', whose leadership is drawn from the hereditary Uniyal priest (Tirtpurohit) family of Kharsali village — the same family that performs the temple's daily worship. This is distinct from the government-run Shri Badarinath Kedarnath Temple Committee (BKTC): the BKTC's founding 1939 Act applies, by its own text, only to 'the temple of Shri Badrinath and the Temple of Shri Kedarnath in district Chamoli' and does not mention Yamunotri. A 2019 state law that would have placed Yamunotri under a new Char Dham Devasthanam Board alongside Badrinath, Kedarnath and Gangotri was repealed in 2021 after opposition from the hereditary priesthood. Char Dham yatra registration, road access to Janki Chatti and pilgrim infrastructure are coordinated separately by Uttarakhand Tourism and the Uttarkashi district administration.

narrative.summaryIntro:
Yamunotri Temple, dedicated to the goddess Yamuna, stands at an altitude of roughly 3,293 m in the western Garhwal Himalaya, in Uttarkashi district, Uttarakhand. It is one of the four sites of the Chota Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath, and is the seat of worship for the Yamuna river, whose true glacial source lies higher up and is not practically accessible.

The temple has no road access: pilgrims reach it on foot, pony or palanquin from Janki Chatti, the last motorable point, roughly 6 km below. Like Kedarnath and Badrinath it is a seasonal shrine, open for about six months a year and closed through the winter because of snow, when worship of the goddess's processional idol continues at Kharsali village. Its administration, however, differs sharply from those two temples: Yamunotri is not covered by the government-run Badrinath-Kedarnath Temple Committee, and is instead managed through a temple committee led by the hereditary Uniyal priest family of Kharsali.
narrative.documentedHistory:
Yamunotri stands at approximately 3,293 m (10,804 ft; one Wikipedia article gives 3,291 m) on a flank of the Bandarpunch massif in Uttarkashi district, the westernmost of the four Chota Char Dham shrines. The true source of the Yamuna is the Yamunotri (Champasar) Glacier on Kalind Parvat, at roughly 4,421 m; because that site is not practically accessible, worship is instead offered at the lower shrine.

Accounts of the temple's construction disagree. Wikipedia's dedicated Yamunotri Temple article, the Uttarakhand Tourist Care portal and the Uttarkashi district administration's site attribute the present structure to Maharaja Pratap Shah of Tehri Garhwal in the 19th century. Wikipedia's general Yamunotri article and the C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar Environmental Education Centre (CPREEC) instead date it to 1839 under Raja Sudarshan Shah of Tehri; a photo caption on the same Wikipedia page separately credits construction to 'Maharani Guleria of Jaipur.' Whoever is credited, the Yamunotri Temple article states the temple 'has been destroyed twice by snow and floods before being rebuilt,' and the general Yamunotri article notes a smaller shrine existed at the site before the present structure was built. CPREEC describes the standing temple as built of granite in the Nagara style, with a pale-yellow, vermilion-bordered conical shikhara and a small entrance porch; the sanctum holds a black marble image of Yamuna together with a garlanded silver idol, with a white-stone image of Ganga placed beside her.

Immediately beside the temple is Surya Kund, a geothermal spring where pilgrims traditionally cook rice and potatoes, tied in muslin cloth, as an offering before darshan; nearby stands Divya Shila, a rock worshipped before puja is offered to Yamuna. According to a legend recorded by CPREEC, the site was the hermitage of the sage Asit Muni, who bathed daily in both the Ganga and the Yamuna; in old age, unable to travel to Gangotri, he is said to have continued the practice after a stream of the Ganga appeared beside the Yamuna at this spot — pilgrimage tradition, not a documented historical event.

Ritual life at the temple — prasad preparation, puja and aarti — is carried out by the hereditary Uniyal family of priests, based in Kharsali village below the shrine; a member of the family was named as treasurer of the 'temple committee' in reporting on the 2026 season opening. This is a materially different arrangement from Badrinath and Kedarnath: the Shri Badarinath Kedarnath Temple Committee (BKTC), created by a 1939 provincial Act, applies by its own text only to 'the temple of Shri Badrinath and the Temple of Shri Kedarnath in district Chamoli' and does not mention Yamunotri or Gangotri. A 2019 state law, the Uttarakhand Chardham Devasthanam Management Act, would have brought Yamunotri, Gangotri, Badrinath, Kedarnath and 49 other temples under a single new shrine board, but it was repealed in 2021 after opposition from the hereditary priests. Yatra registration, road access to Janki Chatti and pilgrim infrastructure are instead handled by Uttarakhand Tourism and the Uttarkashi district administration through the state's Char Dham registration portal.

The shrine opens only for the pilgrimage season: CPREEC gives a recurring pattern of opening in April or May and closing in the third week of November, while the idol's winter descent to Kharsali is elsewhere described as taking place 'during the festival of Diwali (usually in October).' For the 2026 season specifically, the Uttarakhand Tourist Care portal and news coverage record the doors as having opened on 19 April 2026, coinciding with Akshaya Tritiya; no closing date for the 2026 season had been announced as of the access date of this record.

visitingInfo.entryRules: Char Dham Yatra registration is mandatory for all pilgrims before travelling, via the Uttarakhand Tourist Care web portal or app.
visitingInfo.accessibilityNotes: There is no road to the temple. The road ends at Janki Chatti, the last motorable point; from there the shrine is reached by a trek of about 6 km (roughly 13 km if starting from Hanuman Chatti), on foot, pony or palanquin (doli/kandi), or by seasonal helicopter charter from Dehradun. Janki Chatti, about 7 km from the shrine, also has its own thermal springs, separate from the Surya Kund beside the temple.
visitingInfo.photographyPolicy: News coverage of the 2026 season reports a roughly 100-metre no-gadget zone restricting mobile phones and cameras in the immediate vicinity of the shrine.
visitingInfo.nearestBusStation: Janki Chatti, on the Barkot road (NH 94); reachable by bus/taxi from Dehradun (about 180 km), Haridwar (about 220 km) or Uttarkashi (about 125 km), each followed by the trek from Janki Chatti.
visitingInfo.nearestAirport: Jolly Grant Airport, Dehradun, approximately 200 km
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Yamunotri is a seasonal shrine whose opening and closing dates are announced afresh each year — do not plan on fixed dates. For the 2026 season the Uttarakhand Tourist Care portal recorded the kapat opening as 19 April 2026, with the closing date not yet announced as of this record's access date. Confirm the current season's dates and yatra registration status with Uttarakhand Tourist Care on 0135-2559898, 0135-2552627 or 0135-3520100, or touristcare.uttarakhand@gmail.com, before travelling.

openingHours.notes: Yamunotri is open only for about six months a year. CPREEC describes a recurring pattern of opening in April or May and closing in the third week of November; for the 2026 season specifically, the Uttarakhand Tourist Care portal and news coverage record the doors as having opened on 19 April 2026 (Akshaya Tritiya), with the closing date not yet announced as of the access date of this record. No official source consulted publishes fixed daily darshan or aarti clock times for Yamunotri, unlike Badrinath, where BKTC publishes some slot times.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Geothermal spring associated with Surya (the sun)
shrines.locationDescription: A hot spring immediately beside the Yamunotri temple; pilgrims traditionally cook rice and potatoes, tied in muslin cloth, in the boiling water as an offering before worshipping the goddess.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Sacred rock worshipped before puja to Yamuna
shrines.locationDescription: A rock standing near the Surya Kund; pilgrims worship it before offering puja to the goddess Yamuna.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Yamuna (winter residence of the processional idol)
shrines.locationDescription: A village below Yamunotri and home to the temple's hereditary Uniyal priests. The processional idol of the goddess is carried down here by palanquin each winter and worshipped locally for the roughly six months the main shrine is closed.

poojas.description: Prasad preparation, puja and aarti are performed by priests of the hereditary Uniyal family. No official or government source consulted publishes specific clock times for daily darshan or aarti at Yamunotri.

festivals.gregorianRuleOrDate: Traditionally Akshaya Tritiya, a lunar-calendar date in April or May; for the 2026 season the doors opened on 19 April 2026
festivals.duration: 1 day (opening ceremony); the shrine then remains open for about six months
festivals.significance: Marks the start of the pilgrimage season. The palanquin bearing the processional idol of Goddess Yamuna is carried from its winter seat at Kharsali to the Yamunotri shrine, accompanied by Vedic rituals performed by the hereditary Uniyal priests.
festivals.processionOrRituals: A palanquin (palki) procession carries the idol from Kharsali to Yamunotri, with Vedic chanting along the route; the doors are opened with a kapat-opening puja.

festivals.gregorianRuleOrDate: Not fixed; sources describe it as occurring during Diwali (usually October) or, more generally, in the third week of November — exact date announced annually
festivals.significance: Marks the end of the roughly six-month pilgrimage season. The idol of Goddess Yamuna is carried down in procession to its winter seat at Kharsali village, where worship continues until the shrine reopens the following spring.

sources.title: Yamunotri Temple — Wikipedia
sources.claimScope: Altitude (3,291 m); dedication to Yamuna and the black marble idol; construction attributed to Maharaja Pratap Shah of Tehri Garhwal, completed in the 19th century; the temple having been destroyed twice by snow and floods before being rebuilt; Chota Char Dham status; the trek distances from Hanuman Chatti (13 km) and Janki Chatti (6 km); the hot spring said to be hot enough to cook rice and potatoes.
sources.reliabilityNote: Tertiary encyclopedia source, not official. Gives a different builder attribution than Wikipedia's general Yamunotri article and CPREEC; used for history and access, not for any timing.

sources.title: Yamunotri — Wikipedia
sources.claimScope: Altitude (3,293 m) and coordinates; the Yamunotri/Champasar Glacier on Kalind Parvat as the true, largely inaccessible source of the Yamuna; Surya Kund as the most important hot spring and Divya Shila as a rock worshipped before puja to Yamuna; construction attributed to Raja Sudarshan Shah in 1839, with a conflicting photo caption crediting 'Maharani Guleria of Jaipur'; a small shrine existing at the site before the present temple.
sources.reliabilityNote: Tertiary encyclopedia source; internally inconsistent on who built the temple (text credits Sudarshan Shah, a caption credits Maharani Guleria of Jaipur), which is recorded here as a genuine conflict rather than resolved.

sources.title: Kharsali — Wikipedia
sources.claimScope: Kharsali as the village the Yamunotri priests hail from and the winter home of the temple's deity; the idol being brought down from the temple, a four-mile trek away, during the festival of Diwali (usually in October), and returning in spring around April.
sources.reliabilityNote: Tertiary encyclopedia source; describes the winter descent as tied to Diwali, which is not fully consistent with CPREEC's more general 'third week of November' closing pattern — recorded as a conflict on the festivals entry for the closing.

sources.title: Uttarakhand Chardham Devasthanam Management Act, 2019 — Wikipedia
sources.claimScope: The 2019 Act's aim of bringing Badrinath, Kedarnath, Gangotri, Yamunotri and 49 other temples under a single proposed shrine board; the Act's repeal, announced in 2021 following the report of a high-power committee; that prior to the Act, Badrinath and Kedarnath (not Yamunotri) were governed by the Shri Badarinath-Kedarnath Mandir Samiti.
sources.reliabilityNote: Tertiary encyclopedia source summarizing a state law and its repeal; used to establish that Yamunotri was never brought under a shrine board, not to establish current governance detail beyond that.

sources.title: The U.P. Shri Badrinath and Shri Kedarnath Temples Act, 1939 — full text
sources.publisherOrAuthority: IndianKanoon (reproducing the U.P. Act No. 16 of 1939)
sources.claimScope: That the Act, and the definition of 'the Temple' in section 3(d), applies only to 'the temple of Shri Badrinath and the Temple of Shri Kedarnath in district Chamoli' and their scheduled appurtenant shrines, with no mention anywhere of Yamunotri or Gangotri.
sources.reliabilityNote: Primary legal text reproduced by a private legal-database site, not a government portal itself; used only to confirm the Act's scope does not extend to Yamunotri.

sources.title: Yamunotri Dham — Register for Char Dham & Hemkund Sahib Yatra Online
sources.publisherOrAuthority: Tourist Care Uttarakhand, Government of Uttarakhand
sources.claimScope: The 2026 kapat opening date of 19 April 2026 (with daily opening/closing times and aarti schedule stated as not yet announced, and no winter closing date given); altitude (3,293 m); route distances and durations from Dehradun, Haridwar and Uttarkashi via Barkot to Janki Chatti, the last motorable point; helicopter charter, pony, palki and doli options for the trek; helpline numbers 0135-2559898, 0135-2552627 and 0135-3520100 and email touristcare.uttarakhand@gmail.com; mandatory Char Dham Yatra registration via the Tourist Care portal/app.
sources.reliabilityNote: Official Uttarakhand government registration and tourist-care portal for the Char Dham yatra. Live page; season-specific details (opening date, helpline) can change and should be reconfirmed close to travel.

sources.title: Yamunotri Dham — Uttarkashi district tourist places
sources.publisherOrAuthority: Uttarkashi District Administration, Government of Uttarakhand
sources.claimScope: Altitude (3,293 m) and description as the westernmost Char Dham shrine on a flank of Bandarpunch Parvat; distance of 130 km from Uttarkashi headquarters; access via NH 94 through Barkot; nearest airport Jolly Grant, Dehradun, about 200 km away; thermal springs at Janki Chatti, 7 km from the shrine; construction attributed to Maharaja Pratap Shah of Tehri Garhwal.
sources.reliabilityNote: Official district administration website; undated content, no timings given.

sources.title: Char Dham Yatra 2026 Begins: Doors Of Gangotri, Yamunotri Dham Temple Open
sources.claimScope: The Yamunotri Dham doors opening on Sunday, 19 April 2026 (Akshaya Tritiya), with the idol opening to devotees at 12:35 PM; Pradeep Uniyal, described as treasurer of the temple committee, confirming the opening rituals; the palanquin procession from Kharsali village; a roughly 100-metre no-gadget zone restricting mobile phones and cameras; medical staffing for the season.
sources.reliabilityNote: News report on a specific day's events, not an ongoing official record; used only for the 2026 opening date, the temple-committee reference and the no-gadget zone, not for any recurring or general claim.

sources.title: Yamunotri
sources.publisherOrAuthority: C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar Environmental Education Centre (CPREEC)
sources.claimScope: Construction attributed to Raja Sudarshan Shah of Tehri in 1839; granite construction in the Nagara style with a pale-yellow, vermilion-bordered conical shikhara and entrance porch; the sanctum's black marble Yamuna idol, a garlanded silver idol, and a white-stone image of Ganga beside her; the Uniyal family of priests performing prasad, puja and ritual duties; the temple opening in April/May and closing in the third week of November, with the deity relocated to Kharsali; Surya Kund as a hot spring near the temple used for cooking offerings; Divya Shila as a rock worshipped before puja to Yamuna; the legend of the sage Asit Muni and the appearance of a stream of the Ganga beside the Yamuna.
sources.reliabilityNote: Heritage-documentation page from an environmental education centre; undated, framed as general/recurring description rather than a specific season's schedule. Gives a different builder attribution than Wikipedia's dedicated Yamunotri Temple article and government sources.
